The Work, Thought and Torah Legacy of Rabbi Avraham Saba: A Historical, Exegetical and Kabbalistic Study
Introduction and Period of Activity: The Sages of Spain in the Shadow of Rupture and Wandering
The end of the fifteenth century and the beginning of the sixteenth mark one of the most dramatic and harrowing chapters in the spiritual history of the Jewish people [cite: 1]. The decrees of 5454 (1391), the Expulsion from Spain in 5252 (1492), and the decrees of forced conversion and baptism in Portugal in 5257 (1497) caused a deep convulsion in the world of Iberian Jewry [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5]. Within this reality of physical destruction and theological crisis, the spiritual stature of Rabbi Avraham ben Yaakov Saba (5200–5269 / approximately 1440–1508) stands out, one of the greatest preachers, kabbalists and commentators of the generation of the Expulsion [cite: 2, 3, 4, 6].
Rabbi Avraham Saba's enterprise is not confined to the composition of an extensive Torah literature, but constitutes a living bridge between the rich homiletic and kabbalistic tradition of Castile and Portugal and the new centers of Torah that arose in North Africa, in the Ottoman Empire and in Europe [cite: 1, 3, 7]. A distinctive feature, almost without parallel in Jewish history, is the manner in which his works were written: after his original manuscripts were taken from him and torn up or buried in the soil of Portugal, he managed to reconstruct the main points of his works from memory alone during his stay in Fez and in Adrianople [cite: 2, 3, 6, 7]. His exegetical and intellectual teaching, which blends peshat, derash, halakha and sod, gave theological meaning to suffering and became one of the central sources of inspiration for the commentators of the Renaissance and for the sages who were active in later generations [cite: 8, 9, 10, 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life: From Portugal and Lisbon to the Last Days of the Voyage
Rabbi Avraham Saba was born in the city of Zamora in the region of Castile, Spain, around the year 5200 (1440), into a distinguished family [cite: 2, 3, 6, 12, 13]. In Castile he acquired his Torah from the sages of the generation and began to stand out as a charismatic preacher and a spiritual leader who led his community according to the foundations of the revealed and the hidden [cite: 3, 5, 13, 14]. When the Catholic Monarchs published the edict of expulsion in 5252 (1492), Saba was forced to leave his homeland and set out together with his community for neighboring Portugal, where he settled in the city of Guimarães, near Porto [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5, 15]. In Portugal he enjoyed a brief period of five years of relative stability, in which he succeeded in re-establishing his library, preaching before the public of refugees and completing the formulation of his first works [cite: 5, 13].
The period of calm was shattered in 5257 (1497), when Manuel I, king of Portugal, proclaimed decrees of forced conversion and in effect cancelled the possibility of leaving the country [cite: 3, 4, 5, 7]. Under these decrees, the two youngest sons of Rabbi Avraham Saba were seized and forcibly baptized [cite: 2, 3, 4, 7]. In an attempt to save his literary work, Saba fled toward Lisbon [cite: 3, 7, 15]. But following a further royal decree imposing the death penalty on every Jew found in possession of Hebrew books or sacred objects, he was forced to bury his precious manuscripts, among them his commentaries on the Torah, on the Megillot and on tractate Avot, together with his tefillin, beneath an olive tree outside the walls of Lisbon [cite: 2, 5, 7, 14, 16, 17].
After burying the books, Saba was arrested in Lisbon, severely tortured by the authorities and imprisoned for about six months [cite: 2, 3, 7, 14]. When, upon his release, he tried to dig beneath the olive tree to retrieve his writings, he was caught again, flogged and put on board a rickety ship sailing to North Africa [cite: 7, 11, 14, 17]. Arriving in the city of Fez in Morocco destitute and broken in body, he fell into a severe illness [cite: 7, 11, 14]. After he recovered, he began a monumental project of reconstruction, in the course of which he set down his commentaries in writing from his meager memory [cite: 2, 7]. In Fez he lived for about ten years, and afterwards he continued his wanderings to Tlemcen in Algeria and to Adrianople in the Ottoman Empire, where he settled and continued to teach and to write [cite: 3, 4, 6, 7].
The question of the place of his death and its circumstances has received extensive historical and exegetical documentation. The central tradition, mentioned in the book "Divrei Yosef" and cited at length by the Chida in his book "Shem HaGedolim," relates that in the year 5269 (1508) Saba sailed on a ship on his way to Italy [cite: 3, 6, 7, 11]. During the voyage a severe storm broke out that threatened to sink the ship [cite: 3, 6, 11]. The captain turned to Rabbi Avraham Saba asking for salvation, and Saba promised him that the sea would calm on condition that he swear to bring him to burial in a Jewish grave and not to throw him into the depths [cite: 3, 6, 11]. After Saba prayed and the sea grew calm, he died two days later (on the 9th of Tishrei, the eve of Yom Kippur) [cite: 3, 6, 11, 12]. The captain kept his word and brought his body to burial with great honor in the community of Verona in Italy [cite: 3, 6, 7, 11]. Alongside this tradition, some Eastern sages and historians have alternative references linking his last days or his resting place to Fez in Morocco, as a reflection of his prolonged stay and his immense influence on the sages of North Africa [cite: 7, 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers, His Torah Circle and His Family Ties
The spiritual development of Rabbi Avraham Saba was nourished directly from the Castilian beit midrash of the fifteenth century. His foremost teacher was Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon, one of the great sages of Spain and one of its spiritual leaders [cite: 3, 6, 9, 14]. Saba harbored immense admiration for his teacher and cites from his novellae and from what he heard from him in the commentary "Tzror HaMor" in the singular form: "And the clearest of them all is what I heard from the all-encompassing sage Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon" [cite: 18]. Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon bequeathed to his student an integrated approach that sees talmudic halakha and the wisdom of the hidden as one organic whole.
The importance of Rabbi Avraham Saba in the transmission of the Torah tradition is also expressed in the family and student chain that continued his path. His son, Rabbi Yitzchak Saba, survived the hardships of the Expulsion and settled in the Torah centers of Salonica and Adrianople [cite: 6, 19]. The daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak, the granddaughter of Rabbi Avraham Saba, married our master Rabbi Yosef Karo, author of the "Shulchan Arukh" and the "Beit Yosef" [cite: 6, 19]. This family connection constitutes an essential linking element: through it the traditions of homiletics and Kabbalah of Castile seeped from the beit midrash of Saba into the heart of the halakhic and spiritual center that took shape in Safed in the sixteenth century, and influenced the sages of the generation of ordination and Kabbalah [cite: 1, 6, 19].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Literary Corpus: From Lost Works to Reconstruction from Memory
The literary work of Rabbi Avraham Saba encompasses all the fields of Torah: biblical exegesis, the Megillot, tractates of the Sages, halakha, the kavanot of prayer and homiletic books [cite: 2, 6, 7, 8]. He was forced to reconstruct most of his works from memory, noting in his introductions and in the course of his commentaries the days of tranquility in Portugal in contrast to the suffering he endured [cite: 2, 7, 13].
His central and best-known book is "Tzror HaMor" on the Torah [cite: 2, 7, 17]. The work is arranged according to the weekly Torah portions and includes a broad exposition that blends peshat, the midrashim of the Sages, halakhot and secrets drawn from the Zohar [cite: 2, 8, 9]. The name of the book derives from the verse "A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me" (Song of Songs 1:13), as an allusion to the bitterness of suffering and to devotion to God [cite: 20]. The work won great admiration and was first printed in Venice in 5283 (1523) by the printer Daniel Bomberg, and since then it has been printed in many editions and has become a foundational book in the batei midrash [cite: 9, 10, 11, 17].
Another central work is "Eshkol HaKofer," the comprehensive exposition of the five Megillot [cite: 2, 7]. Its parts on the Scroll of Ruth and the Scroll of Esther were printed in stages of the modern period, while sections of his commentaries on Song of Songs, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes remained in manuscript and were printed in scholarly and annotated editions in later years [cite: 7, 21]. Alongside it he composed "Tzror HaChaim," a kabbalistic-ethical commentary on tractate Avot and on the order of the prayers and blessings, in which he analyzes the structure of prayer according to the system of the sefirot [cite: 4, 6, 7].
Other works from Saba's pen are mentioned in the Torah and historical literature. The work "Tzror HaKesef," which was written in his youth in Spain and dealt with the laws of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and idolatry according to the way of the secret, was lost in Portugal and he was unable to reconstruct it [cite: 3, 6, 7, 13, 14]. In addition, bibliographic traditions attribute to him the work "Eshel Avraham" (a name that also serves as a general designation for his expositions and sermons in manuscript), alongside commentaries on Job and Psalms that were lost in the course of his wanderings [cite: 4, 6, 7]. Recent studies also attribute to him an abridgement of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol ("Kitzur SeMaG") [cite: 6].

Tzror HaMor | Comprehensive exegesis of the Torah (peshat, derash, halakha and sod) [cite: 2, 8, 9] | Lost in Lisbon, reconstructed from memory in Fez/Adrianople [cite: 2, 3, 7] | Venice 5283 (1523) [cite: 9, 17], Venice 5306 (1546) [cite: 10], Oz VeHadar [cite: 22, 23]
Eshkol HaKofer | Commentary on the Megillot (Ruth, Esther, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes) [cite: 7] | Lost in Portugal, reconstructed from memory in North Africa [cite: 2, 7] | Jerusalem printings, Machon Yerushalayim/Oz VeHadar [cite: 21, 23]
Tzror HaChaim | Commentary on tractate Avot and the kavanot of the order of prayer [cite: 4, 7] | Lost, partially reconstructed, preserved in manuscripts [cite: 6, 7] | Yad Ben-Zvi edition, Bnei Brak 5775 [cite: 6, 7]
Tzror HaKesef | Laws of the Days of Awe and idolatry according to the way of the secret [cite: 3, 7, 14] | An early work written in Castile and lost entirely [cite: 7, 13, 14] | Lost [cite: 6, 7, 13]
Eshel Avraham / Other Commentaries | Sermons, expositions of Scripture (Job, Psalms) and the abridgement of the SeMaG [cite: 4, 6, 7] | Some were lost in exile and some were preserved as fragments [cite: 4, 6, 7] | Manuscripts and annotated fragments [cite: 4, 6, 7]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Exegetical and Intellectual Teaching: The Relations of Peshat, Derash, Halakha and Sod
The exegetical method of Rabbi Avraham Saba in "Tzror HaMor" and in his other works is based on an integrative conception of the biblical text [cite: 2, 8, 9]. Saba sees no contradiction between the revealed and the hidden, but understands the peshat as an outer shell and the kabbalistic secret as the inner content that gives the peshat its spiritual vitality [cite: 2, 9, 24]. In each portion he opens by clarifying textual and structural difficulties, continues with moral sermons that were originally delivered before the public on Sabbaths and festivals, incorporates halakhic discussions on the customs of prayer and the commandments, and concludes by exposing the mystical substrate drawn from the Zohar [cite: 2, 8, 9, 13, 25].
A central pillar of his intellectual teaching is the theology of suffering and destruction [cite: 1, 13]. Saba processes the national and personal crisis of the Expulsion through the prism of the justification of the divine judgment and a cosmic clarification [cite: 11, 20]. In his commentary on Song of Songs and on the portions of rebuke, he explains that the sufferings that befell Spanish Jewry are not a sign of God's abandonment, but a refining and purifying process of "sufferings of love" [cite: 20]. This position enabled the refugees of the Expulsion to find deep religious meaning in their suffering and to preserve their identity of faith [cite: 1, 11].
With regard to his attitude to medieval philosophy, Saba presents a firm critical position [cite: 1, 26]. He does display familiarity with the philosophical literature, but argues that the exclusive reliance on Aristotelian rationalism failed at the moment of the test of the decrees of forced conversion [cite: 1, 26]. In his view, only simple faith and rooted mystical apprehension gave the exiles the strength of spirit to give up their lives for the sanctification of the Name, whereas abstract philosophical engagement weakened the standing firm in the test of faith [cite: 1, 7, 26].
The Exegetical Dimension | Manner of Application in the Writings of Rabbi Avraham Saba | Sources of Inspiration and Method
Peshat Exegesis | Meticulous analysis of the sequence of verses, resolution of syntactic and substantive difficulties [cite: 9, 24] | Classical Spanish exegesis, grammar and the structure of the portion [cite: 8, 18]
Derash and Ethics | Incorporation of public sermons dealing with the refinement of character traits, faith and the justification of the divine judgment [cite: 8, 13, 20] | Midrashim of the Sages, Tanchuma, Bereshit Rabbah and Mekhilta [cite: 8, 13, 20]
The Halakhic Layer | Clarification of the reasons for the commandments, selected laws and customs of prayer and the synagogue [cite: 6, 8, 25] | Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud, Castilian rulings [cite: 8, 13, 27]
Sod and Kabbalah | Exposition of verses and commandments according to the system of the sefirot and the secrets of Kabbalah [cite: 2, 9, 13] | The Zohar, the Kabbalah of Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon [cite: 2, 3, 9, 18]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Influence and Legacy for Generations: From the Sages of Safed to Research and Editions of Our Day
The importance of Rabbi Avraham Saba and his influence on the development of Torah literature are evident over hundreds of years. His work "Tzror HaMor" became a first-rate source for the greatest preachers and kabbalists of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries [cite: 10, 23, 28]. Rabbi Moshe Alshich (the Holy Alshich) in Safed adopted Saba's method of questions and derash, and incorporated ideas from his commentaries into his expositions of Scripture [cite: 10, 23]. Rabbi Isaiah HaLevi Horowitz (the Holy Shelah) cites extensively from "Tzror HaMor" in his book "Shnei Luchot HaBrit," in particular on matters of the kavanot of the commandments, ethics and the festivals of the year [cite: 23, 28].
In the bibliographic and historical literature Saba earned a place of honor. The Chida in his book "Shem HaGedolim" recalls him with extreme admiration, preserving the story of his self-sacrifice and the wondrous circumstances of his death [cite: 3, 6, 11]. His commentaries continued to be studied in the batei midrash of the East and of Europe alike, as a representative model of profound kabbalistic homiletics [cite: 8, 9, 10, 11].
In modern times his figure has enjoyed a renewed flourishing both in the Torah world and in academic research. In historical and intellectual research, scholars such as Prof. Avraham Gross and Prof. Dov Schwartz have analyzed the whole of his writings, pointed out his contribution to the shaping of the identity of the exiles of Spain, and presented his spiritual world as a bridge between the period of the Golden Age and the new chapter of Kabbalah in the East [cite: 1, 29, 30]. At the same time, in the Torah world, adorned, corrected and vocalized editions of "Tzror HaMor," "Eshkol HaKofer" and "Tzror HaChaim" were published by prominent institutes (such as Oz VeHadar, Machon Yerushalayim and Yad Ben-Zvi), which returned his teaching to the heart of study in the batei midrash [cite: 6, 22, 23, 31].
A particularly symbolic and moving event took place in 2017, when a rare copy of the first edition of "Tzror HaMor" (Venice 5283/1523 printing) was returned to Lisbon in Portugal [cite: 17]. This historic closing of a circle, in which Saba's work was returned to the city where he was forced to bury his writings beneath the olive tree about five hundred years earlier, breathed new life into the story of his self-sacrifice and his Torah legacy [cite: 2, 7, 17].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
Rabbi Avraham Saba, of blessed memory, stands in the annals of Israel as a clear symbol of spiritual strength, self-sacrifice and creativity that did not yield to the waves of destruction [cite: 2, 7, 11]. Out of the depths of personal and national loss, the loss of his children, the tearing of his library and the torments of the body, he succeeded in establishing from memory alone a splendid Torah corpus that nourished Jewish thought for generations [cite: 2, 3, 7, 10].
His teaching in "Tzror HaMor" and in his other works is not merely an exegetical sum, but a living and consoling theology that unites peshat and sod, judgment and mercy, mourning for the past and firm hope for redemption [cite: 1, 8, 9, 20]. His legacy continues to shine in the batei midrash and in the research institutes, as a decisive testimony to the human spirit and to the eternity of the Torah [cite: 1, 17, 23].
